teaser: So much can happen before we see a leaf.
title: A bean becomes.
question: So much can happen before we see a leaf.
idea: A bean holds a tiny plant and stored food. Roots, shoots, and leaves each have work to do.

curiosity.intro: Start with a question. Look for a little while. There is no hurry to know.

questions.question: What is waking up inside this little bean?
questions.notice: Look inside the seed coat. What might those two pale halves be keeping safe?
questions.say: A tiny plant is already inside. The bean holds food to help it begin.
questions.try: Curl one hand like a seed. Slowly uncurl a finger for its first root.

questions.question: How does a root find its way when it cannot see?
questions.notice: Follow the white root down. Now follow the little shoot up. What do you notice?
questions.say: The root does not need eyes. It responds to gravity, which helps it grow down.
questions.try: Trace the two directions in the air: root down, shoot up.

questions.question: What can a leaf do that a seed cannot?
questions.notice: Find the three notes around the leaves. Where does each arrow lead?
questions.say: Green leaves use light, water, and part of the air to make new food. The seed began with food stored inside.
questions.try: Trace a path from the roots to a leaf. Then point to the light.

questions.question: How could we notice a change too slow to watch?
questions.notice: Find the earlier mark and today's tip. What could a drawing help us remember?
questions.say: We can compare notes from different days. Growth can happen too slowly for our eyes to catch it happening.
questions.try: Hold a finger at the earlier mark. With your other hand, show the space up to today's tip.

plates.title: A beginning inside
plates.alt: Big and Little Wonderer look into an illustrated pot cutaway. A split bean holds two pale food stores and a first root pointing down.
plates.caption: An imagined window into the soil. The seed is enlarged to help us see.

plates.title: Two ways to grow
plates.alt: The same windowsill pot shows a young shoot above the soil and a long branching root below. Notes say shoot up and root down.
plates.caption: Roots and shoots respond to their surroundings. Plants do not need eyes.

plates.title: Leaves in the light
plates.alt: Two open green bean leaves meet arrows for light and air. A water arrow leads up the stem from roots below the soil.
plates.caption: Leaves make new food using light, water, and carbon dioxide from the air.

plates.title: A change worth keeping
plates.alt: A leafy bean stands beside a measuring stick with an earlier mark below today's tip. An open notebook holds two plant sketches.
plates.caption: Compare from the soil level. This painted stick is not a scale ruler.

reading.title: The quiet work of growing
reading.coverText: A little bean. A big beginning. Grown-up reads; little wonderer turns the page.
reading.parentNote: About 15 min: look at the scenes, read the six short beats, then talk. Ask what changed in your child's idea. Point, speak, or pause; no independent reading required.

beats.title: Small, but not empty
beats.passage: Little Wonderer looks at the bean. “Is anything in there?” A tiny plant is tucked inside. Stored food will help it begin.
beats.prompt: Point to the pale food stores.

beats.title: Down and up
beats.passage: With water, air, and enough warmth, the bean starts to grow. A root comes out first. It responds to gravity and grows down. A shoot grows up.
beats.prompt: Trace each path with a finger.

beats.title: A new way to make food
beats.passage: Leaves open in the light. They use light, water, and carbon dioxide from the air to make food. The little plant can make more of what it needs.

beats.title: Too slow to see?
beats.passage: “It looks the same,” says Little Wonderer. Big Wonderer opens their notebook. An earlier mark is lower than today's tip. Their notes help them see a change.
beats.prompt: What did the notebook help them remember?

beats.title: Look back at the beginning
beats.passage: “Did the bean need leaves to begin?” they wonder. Look inside it again. The tiny plant had stored food before it had open leaves.
beats.prompt: What in the picture helps explain your answer?

beats.title: A question to keep
beats.passage: They sit together by the window. Growing takes time. “What might change next?” asks Big Wonderer. Little Wonderer has a new question to draw.
beats.prompt: Tell each other one thing you still wonder.

words.meaning: a young stem and its leaves
look for what is alike or different

questions: What helped the bean begin before its leaves opened?
How did their notes help them notice growth?

math.title: How much did it grow?
math.intro: Look at the earlier mark in the picture. Now use these pretend notebook measurements, all taken from the soil to the plant's tip.

tasks.prompt: On Day 4 it was 8 cm tall. On Day 8 it was 14 cm. How much taller?
tasks.hint: Start at 8. Hop 2 to 10, then 4 to 14.

tasks.prompt: On Day 12 it was 23 cm. In our number story, it later grows 9 cm more. How tall then?
tasks.hint: Add 7 to reach 30. How much of the 9 is left?

tasks.prompt: How many days pass from Day 4 to Day 12? Count the spaces between days.
tasks.hint: Day 4 to Day 5 is one day. Count forward from there.
tasks.answer: 8 days. Count the 8 gaps, not all 9 day labels.

math.extension: Would every real bean grow this much? No. These numbers are invented for our math story; real growth varies.
math.parentNote: About 15 min: 3 to compare the picture and table, 9 to draw or calculate, 3 to explain. Use tens-and-ones or number-line hops. Numbers are pretend; do not measure the illustration.

writing.title: Tell the bean's small story.
writing.intro: Choose a scene. Look closely, say your idea, then draw or write what the picture helped you understand.
writing.draw: Draw the seed, root, or leaf you chose. Label one part and add an arrow to show what it does.

frames.hint: Where does it go? What does it take in?

writing.check: Read it together. Can you point to the part your words explain? Add a capital letter and an ending mark if you are writing.
writing.parentNote: About 15 min: 3 to choose and talk, 4 to draw, 6 to write 1–3 sentences, 2 to read back. Accept invented spelling, speech, or dictation. One careful idea is enough.

answers.label: Math · 2
answers.text: 32 cm tall: 23 + 9 = 32. Add 7 to make 30, then add the remaining 2.

answers.label: Math · 3
answers.text: 8 elapsed days: 12 − 4 = 8. There are nine labels from 4 through 12, but only eight gaps.

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: Stored food inside the seed helps the tiny plant begin, before open leaves make new food. Point to the pale halves in the first plate.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: Their notebook kept an earlier height. Comparing it with today's tip made the slow change easier to notice.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept a drawing, dictation, or 1–3 sentences tied to a scene. Possible idea: The leaf uses light, water, and carbon dioxide from the air to make food.

parentGuidance: Wonder first; explanations can wait. Images are simplified, enlarged cutaways, not photographs or a timed growth record. Roots respond to gravity and other conditions; they do not think or see. Seeds need water, oxygen, and suitable warmth; the bean begins with stored food. Green leaves later make food. No real planting is required. Work together and stop when you have had enough.
